NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.
  • According to recent reports, for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
  • According to recent reports, early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SpaceX’s successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA’s path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

According to recent reports, for SpaceX’s purposes, Saturday’s mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX’s deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

According to recent reports, early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX’s existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

The Starship refueling demonstration has slipped two years since late 2024, effectively a day-for-day delay as SpaceX ironed out technical problems with the vehicle. SpaceX may have turned a corner with Saturday’s first-ever catch of Starship at the launch tower.

Other Starship lander tests are coming next year. The first will be NASA’s Artemis III mission, followed by an uncrewed Starship landing demonstration on the Moon. The former requires no orbital refueling, and the latter will need heaps of it.

Ars recently spoke with Steve Creech, the program manager for NASA’s Human Landing System. In this role, Creech oversees NASA’s contracts with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop crew-rated lunar landers for Artemis.

Recent findings suggest that for Artemis III, NASA will launch a four-person crew to low-Earth orbit on a Space Launch System rocket and an Orion spacecraft. Orion will first dock with Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander for two days of tests, following its launch on a New Glenn rocket. The astronauts will open hatches and enter Blue Moon’s pressurized crew cabin to test the vehicle’s environmental control and life support systems.

Then, the astronauts will return to Orion and undock from Blue Moon to set up for a rendezvous and docking with SpaceX’s Starship in a slightly lower orbit, keeping it below most of SpaceX’s Starlink constellation. Orion will stay attached to Starship for just two hours, and the astronauts won’t enter the SpaceX vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that NASA changed the plan for the Artemis III mission earlier this year, rerouting the flight plan from a lunar mission to a low-Earth orbit mission. This means the Artemis program’s first crewed lunar landing will be on Artemis IV, targeted to launch before the end of 2028.

Industry observers note that so, why is Artemis III seemingly testing so much more with Blue Origin than with Starship? Creech told Ars that a big reason is to maintain SpaceX’s focus on orbital refueling. Blue Origin no longer requires in-space refueling for Artemis landing missions. Also, SpaceX has extensive experience with life support systems with its Dragon crewed spacecraft. Blue Origin has comparatively little.

“The bigger challenges for [SpaceX] were the prop transfer and getting to the uncrewed landing demo,” Creech remarked. “The thing that we’re going to learn more with Starship is, when we dock with Orion, they will have control of the attitude, control of the stack. That integrated stack control will be on the Starship side. So, with that huge of a vehicle, I think we’re going to learn more on that.

“With Blue, we’re going to have Orion control the stack for this mission,” Creech mentioned. “When we get to a later mission, the Blue lander with fully loaded prop will have to control the stack. But with Blue, trying to mitigate risk, we’re going to have Orion do that.”.

Artemis III will be Blue Origin’s first time flying a crew cabin for orbital spaceflight. Blue Origin has experience with suborbital space tourism, but those flights were brief and didn’t require the level of advanced life support necessary for longer durations. Blue Origin and NASA will emphasize those test objectives on Artemis III.

Sources indicate that “I think SpaceX’s part was really, we need to focus on the docking,” Creech stated. “If we added a crew cabin, that would slow us down on the other things and not add to what we’re already doing.”.

The Starship on Artemis III will have a full complement of Raptor engines and a docking port on its nose. Blue Moon will not have any main engines when it links up with Orion on Artemis III, only a set of smaller thrusters for pointing control and minor maneuvers.

According to recent reports, “With Blue, you don’t have a BE-7 engine, you don’t have the cryo tanks,” Creech said. “They’re representing the mass of the lander when it comes back from the surface because we think that’s the most critical case. But it does have the crew cabin.”.

While there’s no Starship life support demonstration on Artemis III, NASA added a fresh milestone to SpaceX’s Moon lander contract to test parts of its crew cabin on the ground. The additional testing involves construction of a prototype crew compartment, called Cabin One, at SpaceX’s test site at Starbase, Texas.

Industry observers note that NASA levied upcoming test requirements on Blue Origin, too. The tech giant looks to launch its first Blue Moon test mission early next year after a monthslong delay caused by a rocket explosion on Blue Origin’s launch pad in May. This version of Blue Moon, known as Mark 1, has a single hydrogen-fueled BE-7 main engine. Future human-rated landers from Blue Origin will have three.

According to recent reports, “One of the things we added into the program in the last year is, we really felt like we needed a test of the three-engine configuration,” Creech stated. The hotfire test of the three-engine Blue Moon propulsion unit will occur inside a vacuum chamber at NASA’s In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio.

In a recent development, this year’s Artemis shakeup did more than change the flight strategy for Artemis III. Engineers also altered the architecture for subsequent lunar landing missions. The updated plans will make life easier for teams working on Starship and Blue Moon. That’s not necessarily the case for Orion.

“Our previous architecture for both these landers required a 90-day loiter in lunar orbit for Orion to arrive,” Creech mentioned. “That was something that, for both of these landers, drove a lot of complexity, and a lot of it made the lander job really hard.”.

The fresh concept of operations removes some of that complexity, according to NASA.

Industry observers note that “One of the things we changed was that 90-day loiter,” Creech noted. “SpaceX, they solved it by saying let’s do an Earth orbit rendezvous with Orion, and take Orion to the Moon. For both Blue Origin and SpaceX, we have updated their requirements to a four-day surface day initially. Before, our initial missions were six-and-a-half days.”.

The six-and-a-half-day surface stay was baked into the Artemis architecture because the Orion spacecraft was originally planned to settle into a long, looping path around the Moon, called a near-rectilinear halo orbit. This orbit was predicated by the expected location of NASA’s now-canceled Gateway lunar space station. That, in turn, was driven by Orion’s inability to reach an orbit closer to the Moon.

Now, instead of rendezvousing with Starship near the Moon on landing missions, Orion will link up with Starship in high-Earth orbit. From there, Starship will propel it toward the Moon.

According to recent reports, what’s still unclear, however, is whether SpaceX will have to refuel Starship at an altitude above low-Earth orbit. A graphic presented by Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, last month illustrated this possibility with a “final tanking orbit” before Starship docks with Orion in high-Earth orbit.

“We’re still working that out,” Creech said. “We’re making progress, but where we actually rendezvous with Orion is still in trade, so that’s why you saw a little bit of fuzziness there.”.

Sources indicate that for missions using Blue Moon, the lander will connect with Orion in orbit around the Moon. Blue Origin’s updated looks do away with the requirement for in-space refueling but will still require four rolls out of the company’s New Glenn rocket, one for the Blue Moon lander itself and three with transfer stages to boost it out of Earth orbit to the Moon.

A new stretched Centaur upper stage for the Space Launch System should give the rocket energy to send Orion to low-lunar orbit, which it could not reach with the current version of SLS. NASA has not determined if the new Centaur exploration stage will be ready in time for Artemis IV. If not, Artemis IV could fly with the last of NASA’s in-stock SLS upper stages.

According to recent reports, NASA is also waiting to decide which lander to use on Artemis IV. In either case, two of Orion’s four astronauts will transfer into the landers for the final descent to the lunar surface for a four-day stay, then take off and return to Orion.

Starship and Blue Moon must each complete an uncrewed landing demonstration before a crewed lunar mission. The landing demos are targeted for late 2027 or early 2028, Creech noted, but they won’t necessarily test everything crews will need when they head for the lunar south pole.

According to recent reports, starship’s elevator, for example, is not part of SpaceX’s uncrewed landing demonstration. Engineers will use a test lab at Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama to check the elevator’s performance in a simulated lunar environment.

NASA did not initially require SpaceX or Blue Origin to prove their landers could take off from the Moon before a crew mission. Government officials later added the lunar takeoff requirement for each company’s uncrewed landing demos.

Recent findings suggest that for now, NASA is leaving the details of the uncrewed takeoff demo up to SpaceX and Blue Origin. During Apollo, NASA’s lunar lander never landed on the Moon before Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin descended to the Sea of Tranquility. NASA did, however, fly a dress rehearsal around the Moon on Apollo 10 that included a test of the lunar module’s landing abort capability.

It has been revealed that “Where we are today is, Blue will land and then do a full ascent back to the rendezvous point with Orion,” Creech noted. “With SpaceX. They will land, they will take off again, get to main stage on the engines, and then they will do another landing on the surface.”.

Recent findings suggest that that could change. Today’s plan gives SpaceX two shots at proving Starship can safely land on the Moon, but it comes with trade-offs.

“When I came into the program, I was like, ‘Why are we not going all the way to the rendezvous point?’” said Creech, who took over as HLS program manager in 2025. “Some of my key people felt strongly we would get more out of the way we’re doing it now. There are others that have different opinions… We tend to have a lot of technical discussion and debate. That point will continue to be debated.”.

Sources indicate that for Starship, orbital refueling remains the key to the Moon. SpaceX’s propellant transfer demonstration will involve two Starships, one released from Florida and another from Texas, docking together in low-Earth orbit and transferring a “meaningful” amount of propellant from one ship to the other, Creech said.

“The first quarter of next year, we will see a long-awaited propellant transfer test from SpaceX, where they launch two Starships in pretty close proximity, actually dock, and transfer, we’re calling it a meaningful amount, of propellant,” Creech told Ars. “That is going to be a substantial learning point if they pull that off, because their architecture depends on propellant aggregation and multiple propellant flights.”.

It has been revealed that the propellant transfer test will mark the first time one spacecraft has offloaded a significant quantity of cryogenic propellants—in this case, methane and liquid oxygen—onto another vehicle in space. It is the culmination of decades of government and commercial research on cryogenic orbital refueling. The results will tell engineers how much of the propellant will be lost from boil-off during the transfer.

That is one reason why there’s still so much ambiguity about how many Starship refueling tankers SpaceX will need to launch to give the Starship lunar lander enough gas to fly to the Moon. Without refueling, Starships are restricted to flights in low-Earth orbit.

The low end of the estimate for Starship tankers is six to eight refueling flights to support a Starship lunar mission. Those numbers come from Elon Musk, SpaceX’s founder and CEO, and fall below NASA’s own conservative planning figure of 20 refueling debuts. Musk’s figures hinge on future Starship upgrades to reach the vehicle’s full potential. SpaceX’s goal is to get Starship’s lift capacity up to 100 to 200 metric tons of payload to low-Earth orbit. Today’s version of Starship, known as Starship V3, is still far short of 100 metric tons of payload capacity.

Sources indicate that for context, a Starship carries 1,600 metric tons of propellant with its tanks full. Refueling flights using future, fully optimized Starships might be able to fill those tanks with as few as six tankers. That is not the case today.

Industry observers note that spaceX is working on a taller, heavier Starship called Starship V4. It will fly with nine Raptor engines, an upgrade over the six-engine variant flying today. In 2025, Musk noted Starship V4’s first launch was targeted for 2027. There hasn’t been a recent upgrade to the schedule for Starship V4.

The initial Artemis lunar missions will use Starship V3, Creech stated.

The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • According to recent reports, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

According to recent reports, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to rapidly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed revision in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials noted this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

It has been revealed that external pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” indicates Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

According to recent reports, “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” claims Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

Industry observers note that matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

In a recent development, still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the organization that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are key nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

Sources indicate that “What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” notes Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

Recent findings suggest that • Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some firm data. The bank claims “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

Industry observers note that • Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

Industry observers note that • Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

It has been revealed that spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

Why does your phone say no service even with a SIM card?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.
  • According to recent reports, the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry.
  • On your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your calls and texts aren't going through, try these recommendations.

According to recent reports, the modern electronic device has made a lot of strides in ensuring that it lets you know when something has gone awry. Things like computers, game consoles and tablets will often find a way to alert you to an issue, which makes it easier to troubleshoot any potential problems that may arise.

On your phone, you may notice one of these alerts in the form of a notification that notes, "No SIM card installed." This can be alarming, as it's possible that you may not know what a SIM card even does. Or if you do know what the SIM card does, it can lead to some worrying conclusions as you try to troubleshoot it.

Industry observers note that fixing a SIM card error is a task that requires some diagnostic detective work, or if you're extra unlucky, some actual physical work. Thankfully, there are a lot of tools, both in your phone's settings and in the real world, that can assist with a potential fix.

Sources indicate that when a SIM card error leaves you without service, the phone will still work and power on; it will just be without its main features. The only thing that needs to be done is to take it out and put it right back in. This is usually caused by dropping the phone or ithe card not being properly seated when it was serviced for you, but you can use a SIM ejector tool to take it out. If you don't have one, something as simple as a paper clip or safety pin will usually do the trick.

In a recent development, it's always worth finding out if it's something as simple as a carrier outage, which is entirely possible. If you have access to another device on a different carrier and it can connect to the internet or make a phone call, that could indicate a network outage specific to your carrier. Asking a local friend or family member using the same service whether their phone is working properly can confirm a carrier outage or eliminate it as a possibility.

Recent findings suggest that your phone may be using an eSIM card, which replaces the physical card with a digital SIM. These are great, but they tend to have unique challenges with international travel. If you're using an eSIM card, the way you access settings on an iPhone is slightly different from Android. On an iPhone, eSIM cards are located in Cellular or Mobile Data in the Settings menu, while Android stores them in a setting called SIM Manager. By turning on data roaming, you may fix any sort of problems you're having.

In a recent development, A SIM card or "no service" error can sometimes be something at a software level as opposed to something being wrong with the card. One of the more common fixes is simply toggling airplane mode on and off. Airplane mode can be found by swiping down from the top of your phone and tapping the airplane button.

According to recent reports, you may also be able to do a quick network reset, which sounds bad but has zero effect on your personal files. Doing a network reset on an iPhone is largely similar to the process on Android. It should be noted, however, that the iPhone's network reset is in the Transfer or Reset section of Settings, while Android stores it in Reset Options, also in Settings. You will need to sign back into your Wi-Fi, however, along with some other connections.

Sources indicate that we all get busy in life, and if you haven't paid your bill, then your SIM card will simply stop connecting to your carrier's network. It may seem like a simple thing, but sometimes the simple solutions are blindingly obvious. If you pay your bill online, check your account to see if you've missed a payment or if your service hasn't been suspended for some other reason.

Industry observers note that getting no service on your phone may not even have anything to do with a bad SIM card or an inactive account. You may just be in a place with limited to no service available, or a cellphone tower may be blocked by something. Move around and look for someplace that you actually can connect, as the error may be a result of poor service in that area.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Kingdom and European Union reached a deal on Friday strengthening post-Brexit ties following a summit in Brussels.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

  • President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.
  • Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.
  • In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also mentioned he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi.

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also mentioned he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he remarked.

He mentioned Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

It has been revealed that “You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he stated.

“We want them to build it here.”.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued upcoming rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and mentioned: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”.

It has been revealed that he added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”.

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump mentioned the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president noted. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”.

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

It has been revealed that “I can’t speak to America,” he stated, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”.

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Sources indicate that trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He remarked Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”.

In a recent development, and he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”.

    #47344. Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1179 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Six products and services Google discontinued in 2026

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1179 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Here's a rundown of some Google tools that ended up in the graveyard this year.
    • Recent findings suggest that google is inherently data-driven, and that extends to its products and services as well.
    • Google Assistant has been phased out in favor of Gemini on mobile devices.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Here's a rundown of some Google tools that ended up in the graveyard this year.

    Recent findings suggest that google is inherently data-driven, and that extends to its products and services as well. The search giant has a tendency to shut down services when it feels they're not serving its broader goals, and this has led to the discontinuation of products as diverse as Google Reader, Google+, Stadia, Google Glass, Google Hangouts and dozens of other utilities over the last 15 years. 2026 is no different, so let's take a look at everything Google discontinued this year.

    Google Assistant has been phased out in favor of Gemini on mobile devices. Google initially targeted the end of 2025 for the transition, but pushed the deadline to September, 2026. This means Assistant is no longer available on mobile devices, Wear OS smartwatches, headphones and earbuds, or vehicles using Android Auto projected from a user's phone. It's still usable on older devices like Nest Audio, Nest Mini, the original Google Home, Google Home Max and cars with Google built-in.

    Industry observers note that google Assistant debuted in 2016 (in the short-lived chat app Allo, of all things), and was integrated into much of the broader Android ecosystem, including mobile phones, tablets, smart home devices and vehicles. It provided a hands-free way to control smart home lights, play music, call contacts, and look up information on the web. Those tasks will now be handled by Gemini.

    Industry observers note that the Pixel Tablet was discontinued in September 2026; the link to its listing now takes you to the Google Store's home page, and Google removed tablets as a category from its site navigation. Google's tablet ambitions have felt half-hearted at times, but the Pixel Tablet sought to change that. The tablet debuted in 2023 for $499, and it came with an 11-inch 60Hz LCD panel, decent hardware and reliable battery life. Google sold the tablet for as little as $250 during the 2025 Black Friday sale.

    Sources indicate that its key selling point was the included Charging Speaker Dock, which effectively turned the tablet into a Nest Hub Max. The dock contained a dedicated speaker and served as a Cast target, allowing users to cast music and podcasts to the device. With the discontinuation of the Pixel Tablet, Google no longer has a tablet of its own; there were leaks pointing to a successor with a 120Hz panel, but that never materialized. With Google now focusing on Googlebooks, it may be a while before we see another Pixel Tablet.

    It has been revealed that google ended production of the Nest Mini and Nest Audio in June 2026, with both products now discontinued. The Nest Mini proved particularly popular after Google revealed it in 2019 for just $50, and the smart speaker offered an affordable way to interact with Google Assistant and play music or control smart home devices.

    Nest Audio debuted in 2020 for $99, serving as the successor to the original Google Home. It featured a fabric design and surprisingly solid audio quality via two drivers — a 75mm woofer and 19mm tweeter — with only the much larger and more expensive Home Max rivaling its sound quality in Google's speaker portfolio.

    Recent findings suggest that even though the Nest Audio and Nest Mini are discontinued, Google will continue providing software updates for the foreseeable future. Google is now positioning the $99 Google Home Speaker as the go-to choice for anyone looking for a smart speaker. The Home Speaker has 360-degree sound, but it comes with a smaller 58mm driver, and features Gemini instead of Google Assistant.

    It has been revealed that as part of a broader rebranding initiative centered around Google Health, Google turned the Fitbit app into a unified health portal in May 2026. Alongside the change, Google also indicated that it was migrating Google Fit data over to Google Health.

    Industry observers note that google is positioning Health as its go-to choice to monitor health and fitness data from existing Fitbit wearables, and newer devices like the Fitbit Air and Fitbit Edge use it from the get-go. Fitbit's Web APIs have also been wound down, so if you're using a Fitbit fitness band or smartwatch, you will need to install and use Google Health to monitor metrics. While Health has a lot of features — including an AI-assisted Health Coach — it lacks the social features that made Fitbit's app stand out.

    In January 2026, Google confirmed that it was ending the service, noting that it didn't "provide helpful next steps," and that it would instead focus on "tools that give you more clear, actionable steps to protect your information online." While there are other monitoring services such as Have I Been Pwned, Google's Dark Web Report was notable because it was integrated into your Google account.

    Industry observers note that gmailify was a feature that let you use Yahoo, AOL or Outlook email accounts with Gmail and access spam protection, search, automatic sorting and other services available within Google's email service. The feature debuted 10 years ago, but it was discontinued in Q1 2026; existing customers will still be able to use it until January 2027, and then it will be wound down.

    That said, Google still lets you access email from third-party accounts within Gmail for Android and iOS, and it uses the standard Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) protocol to fetch mails. The only issue is that you don't get some of the extras, like spam protection. In a similar move, Google ended the ability to fetch emails from third-party accounts using the Post Office Protocol (POP); you'll have to use the newer IMAP standard to sync your mails going forward.

    According to recent reports, in addition to these, Google discontinued several lesser-known initiatives in 2026. Google unveiled in July 2026 that the legacy Google Earth Pro desktop app would no longer be available to download after June 25, 2027. If you've used Google Earth Pro in the past and want to continue using it, all you need to do is download and install the app before June 2027, and it will continue to work even after the wind-down. Google is moving its focus to Google Earth on the web and Android/iOS, and while you can still view satellite imagery and Street View for free, it is introducing tiered subscription plans for access to additional data layers.

    Also, Steam for Chromebooks, a beta program that allowed people to install Steam games on ChromeOS machines, ended in January 2026. Google shut down Pixel Studio, a dedicated app that introduced with the Pixel 9 series and let you create AI-assisted imagery using text prompts, in March 2026. With image generation moving to Gemini, Google is directing users to its latest AI assistant instead. Google clearly likes building new tools and features, and while that means there's always something exciting on the horizon, the downside is that there's no guarantee the service you use today will be available a year or two down the line.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion.
    • Recent findings suggest that in a fresh Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025.
    • It has been revealed that some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that in the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

    Recent findings suggest that in a fresh Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar remarked. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it’s really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”.

    It has been revealed that some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

    Karambelkar’s team spotted a candidate system where this might be happening while searching Andromeda for stars changing in brightness, using the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) telescope at Palomar Observatory and data from NASA’s Near-Earth Object Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (NEOWISE) mission. One giant had been brightening for seven years. “When a star first swallows its companion, it has a very subtle effect on its brightness,” Karambelkar remarked. “It slowly brightens, and a lot of light comes out in the infrared.”.

    In April 2025, Karambelkar’s team published a paper suggesting that this system, named AT 2025abao, was undergoing an engulfment in progress. Back then, though, they couldn’t rule out a competing explanation: a single star with instabilities deep within its core. So, they kept watching.

    The researchers reconstructed the history of the system using observations from about a dozen telescopes and surveys, going back to photographic sky plates from 1989. Until 2018, the star barely changed. Modeling those quiet years revealed a giant late in its life, about 350 times wider than the Sun. Its companion was impossible to see, however. “The giant star outshines the smaller star by a factor of about 18,000,” Karambelkar noted.

    Industry observers note that to get around it, the team estimated the mass of the smaller companion based on the amount of dust the system had shed before the engulfment. The estimates suggested a star of roughly 0.7 solar masses.

    Recent findings suggest that between 2018 and early 2025, the giant brightened two- to threefold in visible light, swelling while its temperature stayed nearly constant. Karambelkar compares the process to a spacecraft reentering Earth’s atmosphere. The companion, skimming through the giant’s outer layers, was gradually seeing its orbit shrink, and the friction was heating up the envelope. The energy released by that drag matched the extra light the team observed.

    Then, the star’s visible light dropped by half while its infrared glow kept rising. NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope happened to catch it in July 2025, revealing that the giant had swollen to some 860 times the Sun’s width and wrapped itself in fresh dust.

    According to recent reports, in October 2025, the star brightened roughly 100-fold in just 25 days, shining like 1.5 million Suns at its peak. “At one point, the rate at which the orbit was decaying became very, very fast,” Karambelkar said, comparing the release of the gravitational energy to an explosion. “The companion just fell very quickly, very deep inside the envelope of the star, and it crashed into the core. That violent crash set off a bomb inside the star, and that explosion caused it to brighten very quickly and eject some of the material.”.

    Sources indicate that the eruption had all the hallmarks of a luminous red nova, a type of outburst known to come from merging stars—but an event the researchers weren’t expecting. “Honestly, our minds were blown,” Karambelkar said. He said that this was evidence that this explosion was a consequence of the inspiraling of a binary companion. What made AT 2025abao special, though, was the giant itself.

    All previously known luminous red novae came from younger stars with dense, tightly bound outer layers, which inevitably drive both stars toward a merger. This one was an old giant with a loose, churning envelope—the setup that can also leave behind a surviving tight binary. To find out if the companion actually survived, the team looked at how AT 2025abao’s energy was spent.

    In a recent development, to predict how such events end, astronomers use a formula with an efficiency parameter describing how much of the energy lost by the sinking companion goes into blowing the envelope away. AT 2025abao revealed that the energy goes to different places at different stages.

    Sources indicate that during the slow spiral, most of the energy escaped as light. In the final plunge, the companion released about a hundred times more energy, but only around 1 percent of it was radiated away. Nearly all the rest went into hurling a tenth of the envelope outward at about 10 times the speed needed to escape the giant’s gravity. The rest of the envelope stayed put, which suggests the companion merged with the giant’s core instead of surviving as a tight partner.

    According to recent reports, “Initially, when the rate of energy deposition is low, the star is able to puff up and adjust to this upcoming energy source inside it,” Karambelkar said. “But once the energy deposition rate increases very swiftly as the companion spirals even closer, the star can no longer adjust itself. At that point, it needs to throw out some of its material.”.

    It has been revealed that the efficiency the team calculated fits values inferred from known post-engulfment binaries. But the formula assumes the energy is mostly spent expelling lots of the envelope. Here, most of it went into flinging a small amount of gas at high speeds. It turned out the formula works as a rule of thumb but misses some of the physics.

    It has been revealed that in AT 2025abao, gas shed during the slow spiral piled up in the plane of the binary’s orbit, so the explosion’s ejecta could expand freely toward the poles even though it was blocked around the equator. That, Karambelkar argues, explains the hourglass-shaped nebulae seen around dying stars. “It had been an idea for a very long time that those hourglass shapes are shaped by binary interactions,” he noted. “It seems like what we’re seeing here confirms that hypothesis.”.

    The team admits it can’t yet be sure the stars merged, because dust formed from the ejected material hides whatever is left inside. “We want to continue monitoring the system for several years, possibly even decades, to watch the dust clear out and whatever is remaining inside emerge,” Karambelkar noted. “That will conclusively tell us whether this merged or the binary system survived.” In the meantime, the team hopes to find many more such events involving stars of different masses and types.

    Telescopes we have today can detect them only as far as Andromeda, but the Vera Rubin Observatory and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope should spot them in about 100 Milky Way-like galaxies within some 50 million light-years. “We can have an influx of several of these events per year,” Karambelkar said.

    Nature, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11221-z.

    Breaking: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.
    • China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
    • Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, stated: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035.

    China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.

    Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, stated: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”.

    China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.

    But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.

    In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang mentioned: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”.

    Experts have mentioned electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.

    While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.

    But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

    Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.

    Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.

    In a recent development, china still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some newly introduced ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.

    According to recent reports, one of the key concerns at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.

    Industry observers note that wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a newly introduced renewable-based power system.”.

    In a recent development, china is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.

    It has been revealed that some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU noted it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.

    Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he mentioned. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”.

    Sources indicate that jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”.

    It has been revealed that negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a latest draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that anthropic became a public firm on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders.
    • In a recent development, at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes.
    • Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that anthropic became a public firm on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

    In a recent development, at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

    Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The organization mentioned that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

    However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The company points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”.

    With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

    Sources indicate that $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

    Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

    Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

    28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the tech giant. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

    The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab says.

    It has been revealed that more than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the company’s need for future capital is still far greater.

    According to recent reports, anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

    Recent findings suggest that all told, the organization has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.

    #47337. Building your own mini PC is harder than you would think

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (703 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Building your own mini PC is harder than you would think

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that building a custom PC is a wonderfully satisfying feeling.
    • In a recent development, as you may have noticed, there are so many different form factors for cases and unique enclosures.
    • Recent findings suggest that unlike larger mid- and full-range towers, the mini PC builds tend to focus on a straight-ahead approach with very little wiggle room for frills.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Smaller size can mean greater effort.

    It has been revealed that building a custom PC is a wonderfully satisfying feeling. Even if you've never built one for yourself, it's ingrained itself into the world of content creation and social media so fiercely that everyone has most likely at least watched someone partially build a PC at some point.

    In a recent development, as you may have noticed, there are so many different form factors for cases and unique enclosures. One of the more interesting ones that has been carving out its own funky niche in the market is the mini PC build. Because of the unique form factors and limited space these cases allow, they come with challenges that make a build of this type a bit more difficult than normal.

    Recent findings suggest that unlike larger mid- and full-range towers, the mini PC builds tend to focus on a straight-ahead approach with very little wiggle room for frills. Things that we take for granted in larger builds, like room for maximum airflow or a larger GPU, become pertinent struggles in the mini PC world.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the core things to understand upfront about mini PC builds is the case itself. What we know as mini PCs tend to be built within Mini-ITX or microATX cases. For as small as they are, you might think they'd cost significantly less than their larger siblings. In a lot of situations, that's true, but Mini-ITX cases also come in a lot of different types. Some of them offer fun bells and whistles, which can run your bill up before you know it.

    It has been revealed that A lot of the mainstream mini computers that you can buy from companies, like Apple's Mac mini or certain models of the ASUS NUC, are built with an SoC — a system-on-a-chip that combines a CPU with a GPU — and RAM sometimes soldered into the motherboard itself. Doing something like that isn't really feasible, but you can get fairly close with some commercial cases.

    According to recent reports, no matter which one you're looking at, it may be reassuring to know that despite their small stature, a lot of them are surprisingly roomy. You're still going to be limited by what the case allows in terms of dimensions and compatibility, but those are all easy to contrast and compare with the official specs or using a site like PCPartPicker to determine if a component will fit in your case.

    According to recent reports, the unorthodox shape and size of a lot of mini PC cases means that while it's entirely possible to fill them with a lot of cool stuff, your approach is going to have to be a bit more economical and predetermined. For most of your situations, a mini ITX case will only accommodate a mini-ITX motherboard, while microATX cases will be able to fit in both Mini-ITX and microATX motherboards due to the micro cases being a bit bigger on average.

    Sources indicate that airflow also becomes something of a problem, as the smaller size of these cases means your internal components have a lot less room to breathe. There's usually very little space once all the guts are mashed inside, and that's especially true if you go for a discrete GPU as opposed to an APU that combines the CPU and the GPU. The prices of most small form factor, or SFF, PC components are also a bit steep.

    SFF power supplies, motherboards, CPU coolers and GPUs can all contribute a surprising amount to the final price of a machine, which may make going for a standard ATX build more appealing. Finding all these unique-sized parts isn't even the most challenging concern when building a mini PC, as the physical build itself can be far more difficult than that of a standard ATX machine.

    There's a lot less room, but you also need to be more careful with the actual installation of parts. A standard ATX build can largely be put together in any order, but mini PC builds need to be put together in a specific order due to the part sizes and clearance concerns.

    Breaking: Moon phase today: What the Moon will look like on November 22, 2026

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Mashable

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that the Full Moon is just around the corner, and tonight the Moon is looking almost completely illuminated.
    • 22, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 92% of its surface visible.
    • Sources indicate that if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Vaporum and Serenitatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that the Full Moon is just around the corner, and tonight the Moon is looking almost completely illuminated. We're still in the Waxing Gibbous phase for now, but it won't be long before visibility hits 100%.

    As of Sunday, Nov. 22, the NASA's Daily Moon Guide tracker tells us the Moon is in the Waxing Gibbous phase, with 92% of its surface visible.

    Sources indicate that if you don't have any visual aids, you can still see the Mares Vaporum and Serenitatis, as well as the Aristarchus Plateau. With binoculars, you'll also see the Apennine Mountains, the Gassendi Crater, and the Mare Nectaris. And if you have a telescope, you'll get to see all this plus the Apollo 14 and 17 landing spots, and the Rima Ariadaeus.

    The next Full Moon will take place on November 24.

    Recent findings suggest that according to NASA, the Moon goes through a complete cycle of phases roughly every 29.5 days. As it orbits Earth, the portion of its sunlit surface visible to us changes, giving rise to the different lunar phases. The cycle begins with a Fresh Moon, progresses to a Full Moon, and then gradually returns to a New Moon before starting all over again.

    Latest Moon - The Moon is between Earth and the sun, so the side we see is dark (in other words, it's invisible to the eye).

    Waxing Crescent - A small sliver of light appears on the right side (Northern Hemisphere).

    According to recent reports, first Quarter - Half of the Moon is lit on the right side. It looks like a half-Moon.

    Waxing Gibbous - More than half is lit up, but it's not quite full yet.

    Full Moon - The whole face of the Moon is illuminated and fully visible.

    It has been revealed that waning Gibbous - The Moon starts losing light on the right side. (Northern Hemisphere).

    Third Quarter (or Last Quarter) - Another half-Moon, but now the left side is lit.

    Waning Crescent - A thin sliver of light remains on the left side before going dark again.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

    The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”.

    “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting claims. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.”.

    The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”.

    TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response.

    Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

    Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the firm is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers.

    The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”.

    Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”.

    According to Finland's Defense Ministry, the incursion happened at 12:34 p.m. local time (10:34 UTC/GMT) off the town of Loviisa, on the southern coast.

    The Finnish military said the Sparta II was damaged ⁠west ⁠of Russia's Gogland island, about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Finland's coast, and later drifted into Finnish territorial waters.

    Finnish ‌Border ​Guard Commander Ilja Iljin later told YLE that the vessel, which is known to have links to the Russian military, was struck by Ukrainian  drones while in Russian waters.

    "At the moment, ​there is no confirmed information ⁠about ​what cargo ​is on board, ​but it ‌cannot be ruled out ​that ⁠there is military materiel on ⁠board," ​Iljin remarked.

    The ship is on a US sanctions list, according to a search of the Open Sanctions website.

    The Border Guard later remarked the crew of the Sparta II was evacuating into a life raft and rescue boat.

    "The [Ukraine] war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas," wrote Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo on X.

    Ukraine has the right to fight against the aggressor," he added.

    The Finnish government has put temporary curbs on aviation and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland.

    The Defense Ministry noted Finland had informed its allies about the incident.

    #47329. How to calibrate your 3D printer (and why you should)

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (760 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    How to calibrate your 3D printer (and why you should)

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Better first layers, fewer failed prints and a few calibration tests worth knowing about.
    • It has been revealed that your 3D printer can spend hours making a part, only for it to detach from the bed halfway through.
    • An uneven bed, incorrect nozzle height and poorly tuned extrusion can cause adhesion problems, rough surfaces and dimensional inaccuracies in an FDM 3D printer.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Better first layers, fewer failed prints and a few calibration tests worth knowing about.

    It has been revealed that your 3D printer can spend hours making a part, only for it to detach from the bed halfway through. Worse, the finished piece might look great but refuse to fit where it should. That's a lot of filament down the drain, all because the printer might need calibration.

    An uneven bed, incorrect nozzle height and poorly tuned extrusion can cause adhesion problems, rough surfaces and dimensional inaccuracies in an FDM 3D printer. Calibration can address those problems on both older printers that need manual adjustments and newer models that handle some checks automatically. It's also worth checking calibration after moving your printer, adjusting belts, replacing a nozzle or performing mechanical maintenance.

    Industry observers note that the calibration process starts with a mechanical check, cleaning, bed leveling, Z-offset adjustments (when applicable) and a first-layer test. E-step calibration (rotation-distance calibration in Klipper) with a heated or printing-temperature hotend is a good indicator on supported printers to see if the extruder is extruding the right amount of filament before flow rate tuning. The temperature towers can then be used to fine-tune filament settings. There is no fixed schedule for recalibration, so repeat the appropriate checks as you change hardware or if print quality begins to deteriorate.

    It has been revealed that start with the hardware. Set the printer on a stable surface, and if that's in a bedroom or home office, check whether the space is suitable for 3D printing. With the machine powered off and cooled, inspect for loose belts or toolhead components, then clean the build plate according to the manufacturer's instructions. If your desk is wobbly, the Calibrate button won't fix anything.

    Then follow your printer's bed-leveling procedure, often labeled Calibration, Leveling or Self-check. Many newer machines from Bambu Lab, Creality, Prusa and Anycubic can measure the bed automatically, something worth considering if you're buying a 3D printer anytime soon. Some models, including the Bambu Lab A1 and Prusa MK4S, can also set the first-layer height automatically. The routines differ by model, so follow your printer's instructions.

    By contrast, certain machines, such as the Elegoo Neptune 4 and some Creality Ender models, have manual adjustment wheels, so they need a little more attention. Follow the manufacturer's leveling instructions, adjusting the wheels until a sheet of paper slides between the nozzle and bed with slight resistance at the specified points. Then run automatic leveling afterward if your printer supports it.

    Finally, print a single-layer square. The lines should touch and appear slightly flattened. Visible gaps can indicate that the nozzle is too high, while raised ridges or scraping suggest it's too close. If your printer allows manual Z-offset adjustments, make small changes and repeat the test.

    In a recent development, for E-step calibration, measure the filament, set a measured feed and compare the actual feed, making adjustments as necessary. Klipper has an equivalent setting called rotation distance, so before optimizing filament flow, it makes sense to check this.

    It's not enough to get the first layer correct. Even filaments made from the same material can behave differently. One temperature or flow setting may be perfect for one spool but cause problems for another. Be sure to check the calibration options in your slicer.

    Industry observers note that bambu Studio includes Flow Dynamics and Flow Rate tests, while Creality Print and OrcaSlicer have their own calibration tools. PrusaSlicer also lets you adjust the extrusion multiplier. You don't need to switch slicers to run a test print.

    In a recent development, A temperature tower test prints sections at different nozzle temperatures, letting you compare stringing, bridging and surface quality. Some slicers generate these tests automatically, while others require a downloaded model with temperature changes configured manually. Make sure those temperature changes are configured. Otherwise, you've just printed a tower.

    Flow-rate calibration is done by testing patches for over-extrusion (extruding too much filament, resulting in buildup) or under-extrusion (extruding too little, resulting in gaps). You can also print a 3DBenchy to examine overhangs and details, or a calibration cube to check basic dimensional consistency. But don't start changing motor steps just because a cube measures slightly smaller than expected. Some annoying factors like material shrinkage, extrusion settings and first-layer squish can also affect those measurements, and so can loose belts or other mechanical problems.

    Proper flow and pressure-advance tuning can also reduce blobs around layer starts and stops, although the vertical Z-seam's position is primarily controlled through your slicer's seam settings.
