    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Choi Kyo-jin remarked he ‘failed to prepare adequately’ for entrance exams, which this year had phones banned and checks for cameras hidden in clothing.

    South Korea’s education minister resigned on Sunday after an AI-assisted cheating scandal that erupted in the lead-up to the country’s key university entrance exams.

    The country has been gripped by fears of AI-assisted exam cheating since last Sunday, when the top scorer in a national tax accountant exam confessed to using a miniature camera and smartphone to achieve a near-perfect score, just four days before the crucial university entrance exam known as the suneung.

    The confession sent officials scrambling to roll out a slew of preventive measures for the entrance exams last week, including blocking public wifi in testing areas.

    But the education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, struggled to reassure the public, and teachers’ unions criticised the government response as belated.

    The annual eight-hour suneung determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

    “The exam concluded without any major incidents … However, as the minister in charge, I do not believe I am immune from public criticism that we failed to prepare adequately in advance,” Choi wrote on X.

    “Now that the exam is over, I take full responsibility and hereby offer my resignation,” he added.

    President Lee Jae Myung accepted his resignation, the presidential office remarked.

    Asked during a parliamentary hearing on Monday whether he was confident that authorities could catch would-be cheaters on exam day, the 72-year-old Choi replied: “Due to my age, I am not confident I could.” His response promptly drew public backlash.

    Choi did not appear at press conferences in the days leading up to Thursday’s exam, where a vice minister instead declared the preventive measures.

    South Korea goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended. The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre.

    Sources indicate that in the aftermath of the cheating scandal earlier this month, the government unveiled that smart devices would have to be turned off and handed in for the suneung, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.

    The government also sent emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sounded at full volume and could not be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.

    Officials remarked 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices were identified during Thursday’s exam, nearly half of which were detected through the emergency alerts.

    If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

    There are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

    An important note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

    Industry observers note that if you find yourself stuck at any step of today's Hurdle, don't worry! We have you covered.

    It has been revealed that white House national cyber director Sean Cairncross will be stepping down from his role, Axios reported. The news comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and as businesses across the country report a flurry of technical outages whose cause remains unknown.

    Cairncross, the president’s principal adviser on national cybersecurity policy and strategy, took office in August 2025. Since then, he has met with top AI leaders and helped the Trump administration make key AI decisions, according to Axios. The outlet also reports that the split between Cairncross and the White House was amicable, and his departure was timed so that the White House could nab a Senate confirmation for his role before Democrats take control of Congress in January.

    In a recent development, cairncross, a lawyer and longtime Republican operative, had no cybersecurity background when the Senate confirmed him 59–35. He previously served as the Republican National Committee’s chief operating officer and, during Trump’s first term, as CEO of the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a federal foreign aid agency. The office hasn’t been around long; Congress created it in early 2021, and Cairncross was only its third Senate-confirmed director. The first director, Chris Inglis, left after about 19 months, and the job then went about 10 months without a permanent director.

    We’ve reached out to the White House for comment.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Trump states he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US.

    Donald Trump has remarked he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

    "We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

    Data centres were a central matter in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

    Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

    "We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

    "Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen.".

    But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

    "I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even stated that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

    Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

    It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

    Washington on Monday revealed firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

    The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

    Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back.

    Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

    As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

    Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

    "You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump remarked.

    "We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets.".

    Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

    Meta has already broken ground on a data centre, external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

    The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

    In September Google unveiled a â¬13bn ($15bn: Â£11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

    Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

    Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

    Google has been contacted for comment.

    #47322. Tech Report: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1142 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1142 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them.
    • The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does.
    • It has been revealed that update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

    The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

    It has been revealed that update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and noted that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.

    It has been revealed that to test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

    The findings are striking. They included:.

    According to recent reports, “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”.

    According to recent reports, although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).

    Sources indicate that the most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:.

    Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

    In a recent development, parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM owners to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

    Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

    Recent findings suggest that as noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.

    In a recent development, last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:.

    The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

    Industry observers note that this wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

    The researcher mentioned he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

    Sources indicate that the blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse.

    A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

    Sources indicate that christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.

    He faces up to life in prison at sentencing.

    Industry observers note that federal prosecutors mentioned south Florida was a hub for planning and financing the plot to oust Moïse and install a president of the conspirators’ choosing. The government said Sanon was the conspirators’ initial choice for Moïse’s replacement. Prosecutors also said Sanon helped raise money for the conspiracy and arranged travel to Haiti and lodging for himself and others in that country.

    Sanon acknowledged in trial testimony that he was in communication at one point with people trying to replace Moïse, but pointed out that the group had moved on to another candidate long before the assassination. He denied any knowledge of plans to kill Moïse.

    Recent findings suggest that sanon was born in Haiti and moved to the US as a teenager. He testified that he worked with churches in Haitian immigrant communities in Florida and the midwest.

    Haiti has not had a president since authorities said that a squad of mostly retired Colombian soldiers killed Moïse and wounded his wife in a night-time raid at their home on 7 July 2021. The poorest country in the Americas, Haiti has a history of dictatorship, political upheaval and foreign intervention that has long hindered democratic rule.

    The election of a fresh president is scheduled for next year.

    It has been revealed that prosecutors remarked the scheme to kill Moïse included paying about two dozen foreign mercenaries with money obtained from US government programs that were intended to help businesses during the Covid pandemic, according to court records. US prosecutors have charged more than 40 people with crimes related to the assassination and a dozen have been convicted, including five who are serving life sentences.

    Sources indicate that the plot to oust Moïse began taking final shape in April 2021, when Sanon met in south Florida with a former Haitian senator and several US businesspeople, according to an indictment. The group agreed that Sanon, once in power, would award contracts to two Florida-based companies – Counter Terrorist Unit Federal Academy and Counter Terrorist Unit Security, collectively known as CTU – for infrastructure projects, security forces and military equipment, according to investigators.

    CTU initially hired about 18 Colombian nationals with military training to provide security for Sanon, according to prosecutors. Conspirators also spent months obtaining weapons and body armor and attempting to build ties with Haitian gangs, officials said.

    According to recent reports, by June 2021, the conspirators realized Sanon had neither the constitutional qualifications nor sufficient popular support to become president. They shifted their support to Wendelle Coq Thélot, a former Haitian supreme court judge who died in January 2025 while a fugitive.

    Sanon was previously scheduled to be tried with four other men who were convicted earlier this year, but his case was separated from theirs and delayed for health reasons.

    This is the best type of wireless earbuds for audio output

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wireless earbud design has evolved in leaps and bounds.
    • Our question today is this: What design actually delivers the best sound?
    • Industry observers note that considerations include the type of eartips, how buds secure to your ear, and noise cancelation features.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What design actually delivers the best sound?

    Wireless earbud design has evolved in leaps and bounds. Some of the earliest models would occasionally lose sync between each ear, never mind questions like battery life or sweat resistance. Now, the best wireless earbuds can last an entire workday and will survive the sweatiest gym sessions. You can even use the AirPods Pro 3 as hearing aids.

    Our question today is this: What design actually delivers the best sound? The industry has evolved to support many different form factors, but not all of them are actually geared towards fidelity. Some may prioritize maximum comfort, particular environments or simply a consumer price point. Make the wrong choice, and the results can be extremely disappointing.

    Industry observers note that considerations include the type of eartips, how buds secure to your ear, and noise cancelation features. We'll also explain when it's worth making some sacrifices, since vanilla audio may be better than nothing at all.

    In a recent development, when it comes to form factor, you'll want to begin with in-ear (sometimes referred to as in-canal) earbuds. These provide several major benefits to audio quality over open-ear designs, beginning with passive noise cancellation. You're blocking most of the outside world, although some noise will inevitably seep through. This positioning also maximizes the perceived volume of each bud, which can help you catch more of the nuances in your movies and music. You should even experience better bass response because the buds are directly rattling your ear and the air inside it.

    From here, further narrow your search to models with foam or silicone eartips. These boost passive cancellation as well as bass response, the latter by trapping frequencies inside a space with increased air pressure. For this reason, it's vital to find tips that form a tight fit. You can sometimes upgrade to third-party tips if the ones bundled with your buds aren't doing the job. Keep in mind that while foam is preferable for sound quality, it's less than hygienic for workouts because it's harder to clean.

    Industry observers note that speaking of fit, it's also notable to choose buds that lock in as securely as possible without becoming painful to wear. When buds are loose, they can break that ever-so-important sound quality seal, even if you have great tips. You don't necessarily need buds with an external clip, but those may help if you want both quality and the freedom to sprint or do hanging crunches.

    You'll also want a design with active noise cancellation (ANC). Passive cancellation merely isolates sound. ANC generates "anti-noise," which partly or completely neutralizing the outside world. This is essential not just for hearing quieter elements in your audio, but also for eliminating distractions such as plane engines or nearby conversation.

    It has been revealed that some people intentionally choose open-ear or bone conduction earbuds, despite sacrificing significant bass output and noise cancellation. The reason is simple: situational awareness. If you're running or cycling outside, for example, you can't afford to block out ambient noise because you need to be able to hear an engine, horn, siren or yell warning you of imminent danger. Many in-ear ANC products (like AirPods) compensate by offering "transparency" modes, but of course, it's hard to beat direct exposure to your environment.

    Sources indicate that bone conduction buds can sometimes operate in conditions where other designs are unusable, such as underwater. Those benefits go out the window with models that add air-based drivers into the mix to improve bass. All bone conduction buds do, however, deliver many frequencies straight to your inner ear, allowing them to remain "pure" despite mixing with ambience.

    Recent findings suggest that you'll probably recognize immediately whether these sacrifices are essential. When in doubt, it's better to default to in-ear ANC buds. There's just no way of recovering the lost fidelity if you opt for something else.

    Sources indicate that california’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening noted the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

    The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public.

    “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the manufacturer may have misled investors,” Bonta mentioned in a statement.

    “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added.

    The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

    According to recent reports, the Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position.

    The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government.

    The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the organization, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.

    Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.

    “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.

    Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

    Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has noted Vladimir Putin is a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

    In a recent development, speaking to CNN, Zelensky mentioned it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

    Before Thursday's historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin, Trump called Putin his "friend" and remarked the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

    Russian attacks continued overnight, with two people killed, including a boy, and 52 injured in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, officials noted.

    Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS remarked 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

    On Friday, at least nine people were killed in Russian strikes targeting bridges in the capital Kyiv and railway stations in western Ukraine - with Zelensky calling the attack the "biggest this year" after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

    The strikes came days after Ukraine had badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

    Hours after Friday's strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

    "They [Zelensky and Putin] both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

    Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

    However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

    "I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he told CNN.

    Zelensky also noted speaking about Putin like he was a "friend" meant "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

    The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the south-east of the country early on Friday.

    Polish Defence Minister WÅadysÅaw Kosiniak-Kamysz mentioned the missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

    This was about 100km from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the coalition of the willing - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another cruise missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

    On Saturday, Polish Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski told the BBC the cruise missiles had guidance systems, so "it is very unlikely that they veered off course as a result of Ukrainian electronic warfare".

    "This is a war in Europe that affects our security," he told Radio 4's Today programme, also referencing similar incidents in recent months across Europe.

    Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

    Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said the military alliance had scrambled its jets in response.

    Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

    Putin released a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

    #47312. Latest Update: 10 things you should never do on your Android phone

    Latest Update: 10 things you should never do on your Android phone

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2506 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Avoid major mistakes that make your Android phone less secure and less convenient to use.
    • In a recent development, if you've used Android for a while, you probably know some of its most important rules.
    • Either way, Android doesn't come with a complete user manual, so we've compiled some of the mistakes you shouldn't make on an Android phone.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Avoid major mistakes that make your Android phone less secure and less convenient to use.

    In a recent development, if you've used Android for a while, you probably know some of its most important rules. But even with an OS that's been around for more than 15 years, myths and outdated assumptions still persist. Or you might be fresh to Android and not totally sure how to best take care of your device.

    Either way, Android doesn't come with a complete user manual, so we've compiled some of the mistakes you shouldn't make on an Android phone. They include ignoring security features and trying advanced functions without understanding them. Follow these, and your Android phone should last years in good condition.

    Why it's bad: Software updates fix known vulnerabilities. Patches in a software revision are often responsive, meaning they protect against attacks that are happening, not just theoretical threats. Also, if you use high-security apps like banking and wallet tools, those services won't work if your phone gets too behind on security updates.

    Who says so: Security vulnerabilities in Android are reported to Google, and Google shares this information confidentially with Android device makers. You can read about what threats Google considers critical on its Android Security page.

    Sources indicate that google doesn't share this information publicly for 90 days, giving vendors time to create proper patches and preventing would-be attackers from taking advantage of the details before people have a chance to install patches. There are a lot of players here: Google is responsible for Android software, then every phone maker adds software to Android devices that needs to be patched. Chip makers like MediaTek and Qualcomm also need to patch the drivers that allow those chips to function properly.

    It has been revealed that what's the best practice: Install every security update as soon as it appears. Also, open the Google Play Store and make sure to update apps regularly — automatic updates are best.

    Why it's bad: When your phone is running too many processes at once, it slows down. That seems obvious, but what's actually happening is your phone is shuttling apps between three internal components: storage, RAM and a special partition of RAM called ZRAM made to quickly store and recall active processes.

    When your RAM fills up, it starts compressing processes so it can cram them into the ZRAM partition. When there's no more room in ZRAM for compressed data, your phone enters a state called memory thrashing, where it repeatedly loads data from the ZRAM and then compresses it back in an ongoing cycle. This causes your phone to slow down and heat up as the CPU drains power.

    Who states so: The Android Open Source Project offers technical details on the so-called "low memory killer daemon" (the software process that stuffs data into ZRAM), and the problems caused when you let that memory fill up with extraneous data pages.

    According to recent reports, what's the best practice: Restart your phone regularly to clear the RAM and ZRAM. When you're done with a heavy app like a game, swipe to close it from the app switcher menu (though you don't need to do this constantly for all apps). Finally, uninstall apps that you no longer use to make sure they aren't running processes you don't need. On Android, even if you don't open an app, it may still run and use your RAM in the background.

    It has been revealed that as another part of core maintenance, make sure to keep enough space free on your Android phone. Running it with maxed-out storage means it has no room for temporary caches and other "helper" data.

    Why it's bad: There is no easier way for bad actors to take advantage of security flaws than from apps that come from outside Google's Play Store garden. One common practice is for bad apps to take advantage of your phone's Accessibility controls, which grant privileges for copying your phone's screen and running apps in the background. Google is cautious about approving accessibility access on the Play Store, which is why bad apps are often found on third-party sites.

    It has been revealed that who indicates so: According to Google's security blog, Google Play Protect identified more than 13 million malicious apps from outside the Play Store in 2024 — and those are just the ones the service was able to detect. The standards for Android app security are set by the App Defense Alliance, part of Linux, which forms the foundation of Android's code.

    What's the best practice: If you must install apps from outside Google Play, make sure you 100 percent trust the source. A first-party developer you trust, or a security-conscious third-party app market like F-Droid, is better than a random forum or Reddit page. Always use caution outside the Google Play Store.

    Sources indicate that why it's bad: If you're asked to disable Google Play Protect for any reason, that's a major red flag. Usually, a scammer will try to convince you to download a phony app by pretending to be your bank or another trusted source. When you try to install the fresh app, you get a warning from Play Protect, which the scammer tells you to disregard. Never ignore this warning.

    It has been revealed that who indicates so: Play Protect has been a part of Android for almost 10 years, and it gets constant updates that make it more stringent. It's the primary line of defense against dangerous apps you try to install.

    What's the best practice: Never disable Google Play Protect, but don't trust it blindly either. Researchers like Bitdefender claim to have found apps that made it to the Play Store and still pose a risk, so you still need to be careful about what you install.

    Sources indicate that why it's bad: In the early days of Android, there were good reasons to obtain root access to your phone. You could enable features that were inexplicably turned off, like network tethering on Verizon's early Android devices. It allows you to remove bloatware installed by your mobile carrier, or even load an OS like CyanogenMod that was better than what Samsung or Google provided. Those days are over.

    Rooting a phone triggers failures in Google's Play Integrity API, and that's a break that can't heal. You won't be able to use banking or financial apps or any apps that rely on your phone's Strong integrity, a tag that disappears when you obtain root access to your system. Having root access means mistakes or malicious apps can cause much more damage.

    Who indicates so: Even the US government says this is a bad idea. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) warns against rooting your mobile device, listing rooting and jailbreaking a phone as a threat in its Mobile Threat Catalogue.

    In a recent development, what's the best practice: There is not enough reason to root your primary Android phone today if you aren't a software developer. Phone features are no longer restricted based on which carrier sold you the phone. And phone makers let you remove (or at least hide) the bloat — you can even remove Google apps that used to be permanently stuck in your app drawer.

    If you have an old device that no longer gets updates, rooting and installing a custom ROM can bring fresh life to it, but the trade-offs aren't worth it on an in-support daily phone.

    Recent findings suggest that why it's bad: Say your new Android phone came with a bunch of apps you don't want. The Settings menu lets you disable them so they disappear, but they're still taking up space and you can't let it go.

    In a recent development, so, you found a YouTube video that shows you how to turn on USB Debugging, which lets you manage your phone's files from your PC. You figure this isn't a problem, since you aren't installing anything from a third party or handing your phone to a stranger.

    Industry observers note that except those instructions often skip an notable final step: remember to turn USB Debugging off. Otherwise, your phone is more vulnerable to attacks using a computer. While Android requires you to authorize the connection when you connect to any PC for the first time, you might not realize what you're doing, or someone could trick you into handing over access. That's why it's important to watch the prompts when connecting to an unknown USB port (more on this below).

    There are lots of features on Android that can give you advanced access to your system without being dangerous, as long as you're careful to turn them off when you're done.

    Who claims so: Google is enthusiastic about Android customers trying Developer Mode, but admits "it's essential to understand the implications of each setting." That's a massive understatement, since these options can cause problems if you don't know what they do.

    Sources indicate that what's the best practice: If you dabble in the Android cauldron, be sure to put out the fire. Disable USB Debugging and any other features that you turned on once the task is done. Follow instructions closely, and don't mess with features you don't truly understand.

    Why it's bad: When you access an open Wi-Fi network, you have no guarantees of privacy. Anyone else who joins the network can use free analyzer tools to see what's happening. Almost every modern website uses HTTPS, meaning information you send to a site (like login credentials) is encrypted. But someone snooping on the network would still be able to see which sites you're accessing.

    Even if the network seems trustworthy, it's hard to be sure. For example, say you use the password on the wall to connect to a cafe network. Someone could have set up a fake network with the same name and password combination, and your device won't know the difference. It looks for the strongest connection, which might be the person next to you with a sketchy hotspot and Wi-Fi sniffer, not the router mounted above the ceiling.

    Industry observers note that who indicates so: The US Government's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency remarked public Wi-Fi networks are one of the biggest threats for high-risk security attacks, though this was in 2012 before HTTPS was as common as it is now. Technology departments at universities like Vanderbilt continue to warn of the risks and how to mitigate them.

    Recent findings suggest that what's the best practice: Use a VPN for another layer of encryption on untrusted networks. If you must use public Wi-Fi without a VPN, avoid working with sensitive info like bank details. And if a site doesn't use HTTPS, leave it for when you're at home.

    Why it's bad: When you plug into a USB port, you are often connecting your phone to both a power source and a data connection. Your phone will prompt you to trust a fresh device for data connections, which is where the risk comes in. If you grant that access, an attacker could steal your photos, load malware onto your phone or intercept communications, among other harmful actions.

    Who indicates so: The FCC has issued warnings against plugging your phone into unknown USB ports. While no reports of so-called "juice jacking" attacks have happened in the real world, the technique has been demonstrated multiple times at hacking events (first at the Black Hat security conference in 2013). There's even a USB cable called the O.MG sold by an InfoSec testing firm, Hak5, that contains the necessary hardware to pull off a juice jacking attack — for testing purposes, of course.

    What's the best practice: When you plug your phone in at an airport, don't accept any pop-up notices that appear. If possible, use a proper wall outlet or a portable charger to eliminate the small theoretical risk of these attacks.

    In a recent development, why it's bad: Apps often ask for more information than they need. Does a calculator app need access to your photos? Does a flashlight app need to use the microphone? Those are obvious examples of permissions you should be critical of. More key are Accessibility permissions, which allow an app to monitor everything on your screen, monitor your SMS messages (for 2FA codes, for example) and even control other apps without your knowledge. That sketchy to-do list app could open your banking app, change your password and have its way with your accounts, if it has proper accessibility access.

    Another permission to watch is Display over other apps. This lets Facebook float Messenger chat heads on top of your home screen and other apps, but could also let a bogus app overlay a fake OK button that gives permission to further abuse. It may look like you're tapping Agree in the Google Play Store, when the button is actually a separate app that will install a nasty payload.

    It has been revealed that who notes so: Android takes permissions seriously: the latest versions of Android revoke all permissions from apps you haven't used in a long time, just to be safe. Google tells developers to ask for permissions incrementally, and only when a feature is needed, so you have context for why the app is asking.

    According to recent reports, what's the best practice: You know to be careful with microphone and camera access, but also be aware when an app asks for any unusual permissions. Regularly review your permissions and remove any that are unnecessary (or uninstall apps you never use).

    Sources indicate that why it's bad: Lithium batteries hate extremes. When one is always kept at 100 percent, it increases the wear on internal components and reduces the total charge the battery can hold over time, according to Samsung. That's why modern iOS and Android versions come with battery management tools that keep your phone around 80 percent while you charge overnight, only topping up to 100 percent just before you wake up.

    You should also avoid using cheap, off-brand USB cables for charging. Your phone came with a high-quality USB cable that includes a controller chip to make sure the device gets a steady voltage. Cheap USB cables often lack that chip, which can cause your battery to overheat. At worst, it can cause internal electrical damage, though any excess heat is bad for your battery's chemistry. It speeds up reactions and can cause the battery to degrade faster.

    Industry observers note that who says so: Most phone makers have a warning page about batteries, with battery utilities recommending that you only charge your phone to 80 percent under normal circumstances. This will extend the longevity of the battery, which is a good idea if you initiative on keeping your phone for many years.

    What's the best practice: Let Android do its job. Your phone has software that helps manage battery, both for day-to-day life and overall longevity. Don't force your phone to charge past Android's recommended limit all the time.

    Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (448 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw.
    • This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
    • Sources indicate that the 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Karen Scarborough (left) and Anne Lindboe got to work with a two-handled saw.

    This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.

    Sources indicate that the 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.

    Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.

    Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.

    Scarborough mentioned: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.

    "This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period.".

    The 21m tree has been nicknamed Jolly Cheery.

    Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square.".

    Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.

    "The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.

    "I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times.".

    Count the rings: Anne Lindboe (left) and Karen Scarborough (right) with a slice of the 75-year-old trunk.

    For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.

    Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.

    Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
    • It has been revealed that well, maybe not all of them.
    • According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left.

    It has been revealed that earlier this week at the DealBook conference in New York, Elon Musk, beamed in from a trip to China with President Donald Trump, was asked about the ouster of his longtime friend, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Musk compared it to kicking Michael Jordan off the Chicago Bulls’ roster during his historic run. Of Nvidia’s employees, he mentioned, “They love [Huang]. They love him.”.

    It has been revealed that well, maybe not all of them. Thousands of employees have signed a letter asking for Huang’s return, but others tell The New York Times he ruled through praise and fear, as well as by humiliating people.

    According to the Times, Huang told subordinates that Nvidia’s wealth meant it wasn’t possible to motivate employees with money, so humiliation was the only lever left. He reportedly told one executive his mother should have aborted him and told another employee he would rip his arms off and beat him to death with them.

    Naturally, over a 33-year career, regrettable things may have been said, but the Times found a long paper trail that suggests the incidents weren’t isolated. In 2005, for example, Michael Winston, a former HR chief, threatened to sue and called Huang’s conduct the most abusive he’d seen. Nvidia paid him more than $1 million. Huang’s spokesman calls the allegations fabrications.

    Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that meta’s executives are rethinking the organization’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030.
    • The tech giant’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta.
    • “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that meta’s executives are rethinking the organization’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Substantial Tech competitor racing to build upcoming AI data centers.

    The tech giant’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”.

    “We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

    Meta’s statement about re-evaluating its 2030 emissions goal is a significant public acknowledgment, given that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft have all stuck by their original sustainability goals so far.

    But all the companies have acknowledged challenges in balancing their original sustainability goals against the breakneck buildout of hyperscale data centers. Despite efforts to invest in more renewable energy projects, Meta and its rivals are still often pushing forward on AI data centers that rely on burning natural gas to generate electricity.

    Meta’s report described the company’s total emissions as surging from 15.6 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent in 2024 to more than 21.7 million metric tonnes in 2025.

    Industry observers note that that would make Meta’s annual carbon footprint roughly comparable to total emissions for the state of Idaho, while surpassing the total emissions of states such as Hawaii, Maine, South Dakota, and Fresh Hampshire. The manufacturer attributed much of this emissions increase to “capital goods,” like as data center servers.

    That also represents a nearly 40 percent increase in Meta’s carbon footprint between 2024 and 2025, which is the highest percentage year-over-year increase for total emissions reported by any of the four major US tech giants.

    According to recent reports, for comparison, Microsoft reported a 25 percent increase in its overall carbon footprint, Google reported an 18 percent increase, and Amazon’s report described a 16 percent increase between 2024 and 2025. However, Meta still likely has one of the smallest total carbon footprints among the Big Tech companies.

    Meta’s approach to achieving net-zero emissions has included developing new renewable energy projects to match emissions and using carbon removal technology.

    But even when factoring in such efforts, Meta still reported net emissions increasing from more than 8.1 million metric tonnes to more than 11.8 million metric tonnes for 2025. That represents a 45 percent increase.

    From a water consumption standpoint, Meta reported progress in reducing facility consumption from 825 million gallons in 2024 to 790 million gallons in 2025.

    Yet that positive trend is tempered by the fact that Meta also described an increase in water consumption from “areas with water stress,” rising from 198 million gallons in 2024 to 246 million gallons in 2025.

    Sources indicate that meta also reported a sharp increase in water consumption related to purchased electricity—the amount of water consumed by related power generation—from 19 billion gallons in 2024 to more than 26 billion gallons in 2025. This once again highlights that, for data centers, the far bigger water usage comes from the power plants that supply electricity to data centers as opposed to data centers directly using water for cooling.

    Still, some minor credit is due. The publication Data Center Dynamics pointed out that “Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.”.

    It would very much be in the public interest for other Significant Tech companies to follow suit on the reporting front—and public pressure continues to build after the AI backlash impact on US midterm election results.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.
    • The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers.
    • Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner.

    The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

    Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

    Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination.

    According to recent reports, the intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially notable since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white.

    One diplomat mentioned: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.”.

    The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres, but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

    Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh, is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen.

    A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills.

    In a recent development, nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month.

    In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”.

    Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

    It has been revealed that some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle.

    According to recent reports, but others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval.

    It has been revealed that it is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible.

    Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE.

    Industry observers note that the two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority.

    Industry observers note that in the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point.

    In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer.

    According to recent reports, grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution.

    Recent findings suggest that although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

    One way or the other, the logjam has to be broken soon.

    Your PC's USB port can charge your phone, even when it's turned off — Here's how

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Your USB ports might have a hidden "Always On" mode that charges your phone with the PC shut down.
    • It has been revealed that almost all PC USB ports supply enough current to charge a device, but not all continue to do so when the PC is shut down.
    • It has been revealed that depending on the system, USB standby power might be on by default or be part of an energy-saving setting that cuts power when the PC is off.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Your USB ports might have a hidden "Always On" mode that charges your phone with the PC shut down.

    It has been revealed that almost all PC USB ports supply enough current to charge a device, but not all continue to do so when the PC is shut down. This convenient feature can also be confusing, since each brand tends to have its own terminology. For example, Lenovo calls it an "Always On" port while Dell uses the term PowerShare. Others stick with icon labels, like a battery symbol or a lightning bolt. The best way to know for sure is to dig into your PC's manual, confirm the markings and learn how to enable it.

    It has been revealed that depending on the system, USB standby power might be on by default or be part of an energy-saving setting that cuts power when the PC is off. Your desktop or motherboard documentation should have this information. Fortunately, testing the feature is fairly simple: plug your phone in, turn the PC off and see if your phone continues charging.

    If it stops charging, it's safe to assume the setting is off, which you can rectify in the BIOS or UEFI on most Windows PCs. (If your PC never supported the feature, changing settings won't help.) Restart the PC and press the key the startup screen tells you to (usually F2, Del or F10). Look under Advanced, Power or Chipset for a USB power delivery or Always On charging option and enable it. If you see ErP (Energy-related Products) or Deep Sleep settings, make sure they're disabled. Save and exit.

    According to recent reports, you don't need a computer science or software engineering degree to do this, just a little patience as you wait for the PC to boot up and press the right key. The menu can be confusing at times, but you're unlikely to brick your PC.

    For starters, energy-saving features may get in the way. Anything that uses standby power will conflict with firmware settings that cut power to reduce consumption. For instance, if ErP Ready is enabled in select ASUS NUC PCs, USB standby power during shutdown or hibernation is disabled. Check your system's instructions before changing anything.

    You also may not have to turn off every single energy-saving feature just to charge your phone when your PC is off. Keep in mind that changing the energy-saving settings won't add post-shutdown charging if the system never supported it to begin with.

    Recent findings suggest that laptops are an entirely different case, since they often come with battery reserve limitations. Depending on the model, USB charging may stop when the laptop's battery hits a reserve threshold. Laptop charging features may depend on an AC adapter after shutdown, and that's a potential restriction that shouldn't be confused with a desktop's standby power settings. Make sure your USB plug is completely in the port and that the cable is reliable, not one that's been sitting in an attic box for the last quarter century.

    Sources indicate that in this context, "Always On" refers to power availability, but that's not the same thing as "charging only." A supported port can continue to supply power while the computer is off, though the wording shouldn't be taken literally. Firmware settings can disable that power, and the behavior may be different between ports on the same system.

    Power and data transfers are also different capabilities. A phone charging while the PC is shut down doesn't mean you can transfer photos from your phone or copy files to it. The specific feature here is all about electricity available via the USB connection.

    In a recent development, another problem is the lack of consistency in names, setup processes and USB port symbols. One system may offer a dedicated USB power setting while another's ports depend on power-saving configurations. Even within a single brand, capabilities and terminology can differ, and manufacturers implement "Always On" USB in drastically different ways.

    For example, "Always On" could mean the feature is active after shutdown, during hibernation or while your PC is asleep. It could mean two of them, just one or all three. The feature may come with symbols, color coding, terminology or fine print in a manual, but not necessarily all of the above.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials stated on Saturday.

    The gang is aligned with the Mayos, one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

    Authorities said the overnight raid resulted in the capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.

    The operation left at least 11 people dead. Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed, Mexico’s Defense Ministry mentioned on Saturday afternoon.

    Sources indicate that the 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.

    He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime. "Chapo Isidro" was once a rival of imprisoned drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman.

    The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military mentioned.

    It was not immediately clear whether authorities would extradite "Chapo Isidro" to the US.

    According to recent reports, on Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies. However, they offered few details about how authorities in both countries coordinated.

    In a recent development, in a post on X, US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson wrote: "Results like these are not achieved overnight. They are the product of sustained cooperation and trust. This is what we can accomplish when we work together. ​We will continue pursuing criminals.".

    The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according to Mexico's US embassy.

    Industry observers note that unverified videos from Guasave, however, demonstrated military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after "Chapo Isidro" was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.

    Mexico's Defense Ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.

    The Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade​​​​​​. Less than two weeks ago, the Mexican Navy declared the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.

    Mexican President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.

    Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years.

    New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

    Mamdani on Friday unveiled a proposal to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

    Prepares to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

    Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

    It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

    It has been revealed that the Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

    It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

    Recent findings suggest that "[B]uilding a upcoming system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association mentioned in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges.".

    "It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in Latest York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she mentioned.

    The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

    Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

    In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani stated Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

    New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the blueprint.

    Mamdani's office said the city would open up four newly introduced jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

    Sources indicate that the mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

    Mamdani mentioned his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

    He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health complications.

    Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

    The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (Â£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

    Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier.

    From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

    If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward.

    According to recent reports, the AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed.

    According to recent reports, the Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages.
