    #47298. Tech Report: This is what can happen if too many devices are sharing your home network

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: This is what can happen if too many devices are sharing your home network

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It doesn’t take much to bring a home network to its knees.
    • Any home network, regardless of efficiency and performance, can get overburdened when enough devices are connected, each vying for its own slice of the pie.
    • According to recent reports, there are two potential limitations to consider.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It doesn’t take much to bring a home network to its knees.

    Any home network, regardless of efficiency and performance, can get overburdened when enough devices are connected, each vying for its own slice of the pie. When that happens, it's pretty obvious, with the infamous buffering circle plaguing screens, laggy online gaming, endless download times and the apocalypse landing on your doorstep. It doesn't take much to reach this point either. A single high-end smartphone can eat up quite a bit of bandwidth all by itself.

    According to recent reports, there are two potential limitations to consider. The first is the internet connection coming into your home via your Internet Service Provider (ISP). The second is the Wi-Fi connection between your router and your devices. A faster internet blueprint won't fix a weak signal from a router tucked into an out-of-the-way corner. On the flip side, a faster router can't do much with a slow internet service plan.

    In a recent development, the knee-jerk reaction is to replace your router, upgrade your internet service plan speed and place the router in a more efficient position. That may indeed help, but not everyone can run out and purchase a Wi-Fi 6 or 7 router and hassle their ISP for faster service and an accordingly higher bill. But you shouldn't have to, as long as you don't mind playing with the numbers.

    There's no reliable rule that states "100 Mbps internet connection supports a specific number of devices." Instead, estimate how many devices can run simultaneously without bogging everything else down. Netflix, for example, recommends a stable connection of at least 15 Mbps for each 4K stream. Three streams represent about 45 Mbps of recommended capacity without accounting for any overhead throughout the home (even coffee pots connect to Wi-Fi nowadays).

    No, this doesn't mean each stream constantly consumes exactly 15 Mbps. We're just using it as a reference number for the purposes of planning things out. If there are 10 devices in the home, each using 10 Mbps, that would equal 100 Mbps. In that case, a 100 Mbps download speed (FCC's minimum broadband requirement) would leave no room to spare if all 10 devices are up and running at the same time. In reality, of course, speeds fluctuate, but it's a helpful little math drill to run if you're trying to stay organized and keep that ridiculous buffering circle off your TV screen.

    Upload speeds are vital for things like video calls or security cameras uploading footage of squirrels fighting in the front yard. Upload speeds are generally much slower than download speeds, thanks to asymmetrical broadband with ISPs allocating most of the bandwidth to downloads. Once you understand the speeds and the average consumption of a single device, you can initiative large downloads or other Wi-Fi-intensive tasks for less busy times.

    According to recent reports, for the vast majority of households, one router is more than enough. A good mesh system or efficiently placed access points will solve most problems. An additional router makes sense in very specific situations. For instance, if your ISP has no choice but to run your wires and install your gateway in the far corner of your home, running an Ethernet cable from the gateway to a router in the center of your home might work out great.

    But your best bet is to start with what you already have, and add to it incrementally on an "as-needed" basis. Switch stationary devices (PCs, consoles, TVs, etc.) to Ethernet, if possible, removing their traffic from Wi-Fi, although their internet activity will still share your broadband connection. A router upgrade is an option if you need something that can efficiently manage more devices. Just remember that advertised device capacity is great, but it can't overcome bandwidth limitations on your ISP plan.

    According to recent reports, if you opt for a mesh system to complement an ISP gateway, follow the setup instructions closely and don't leave both devices performing routing duties without checking the configuration. If the gateway and mesh remain in their default routing modes, it could create double NAT, which might cause an issue with online gaming or port forwarding. It doesn't need to get too complicated because the end point boils down to addressing what is constraining your system. Crunch the numbers first; decide which direction to go second. You got this!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed.
    • Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test.
    • Industry observers note that the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that google’s flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that’s been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

    Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There’s an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The “I’m Feeling Lucky” button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

    Industry observers note that the search button has obviously been a part of Google’s search page forever. However, it wasn’t in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

    The other significant change brings your recent AI conversations to the forefront. If you’re logged into Google, the search homepage will have an expandable sidebar on the left with your recent AI Mode search threads. This sidebar will also be accessible on the results page. According to Stein, the sidebar made a “big difference” in how people made progress on their web searches, calling it a “simpler way to pick up where you left off.”.

    It’s easy to feel frustrated by changes like this if you don’t like Google’s new AI approach to search. But at the same time, the loss of functionality is minimal. Google probably has usage data that shows that particular search button was rarely used. Most people probably just hit Enter or click an autocomplete suggestion to go to the results.

    Industry observers note that this change claims more about Google’s priorities and the future of search. AI features get prominent buttons, and your AI conversations now have a whole sidebar UI. Meanwhile, traditional search is increasingly de-emphasized. There may come a day when AI Mode takes over completely, forcing you to manually select the old-fashioned version of search. It does feel like Google is inching in that direction.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week.

    An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

    Levent AlpÃ¶ge stated, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

    It has been revealed that if found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. AlpÃ¶ge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

    The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months confirmed scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

    As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

    It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

    Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

    Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

    AlpÃ¶ge noted that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

    In a recent development, "The precise timing is horrible," AlpÃ¶ge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier.".

    "I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

    The complete textual proof that AlpÃ¶ge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

    Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

    "I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao stated.

    No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

    Sources indicate that openAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

    More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

    The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

    Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

    A group of maths scholars remarked, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

    "We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars remarked in a group letter.

    A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

    It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

    #47293. A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (827 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    A transcription firm used by police, prosecutors, and tech giants exposed customer data online

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (827 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.
    • Industry observers note that the data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage.
    • According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A transcription company that caters to law enforcement, government departments, and Silicon Valley tech giants has resolved a security lapse after leaving a large amount of internal data, including customer transcriptions and their source materials, exposed to the web.

    Industry observers note that the data security lapse at San Francisco-based Tigerfish exposed transcriptions of police interviews, body-cam footage, and customers’ raw audio and video footage. The exposed data also included invoices of the company’s customers, which include police departments and prosecutors’ offices.

    According to Anurag Sen, a good faith security researcher who found the data, the files were located on an Amazon-hosted (S3) cloud server that was openly listed and accessible to anyone via an easy-to-guess web address — no passwords needed.

    The security lapse underscores how simple flaws or misconfigurations can result in sensitive information getting exposed online, especially as AI makes it easier to uncover weaknesses that can put companies and their data at risk.

    Sen discovered the exposed data online in October and alerted the manufacturer to the concern, but did not hear back. Sen later provided details to TechCrunch in an effort to flag the incident with the company for resolution.

    Sen, 30, is no stranger to TechCrunch. For the past decade, he has searched for sensitive datasets exposed online with the goal of notifying the companies and organizations that their information is open to the internet. Like many security researchers, much of his efforts are driven by a duty to secure the internet, and he describes his work as an “unpaid air-traffic controller.”.

    Given Sen’s propensity for finding often highly confidential information online, we verified the source of the leak and the data, and contacted Tigerfish.

    Soon after making contact, Tigerfish secured its exposed S3 cloud bucket.

    Sources indicate that “We’ve blocked all public access to the bucket you identified, including directory listings and individual files,” Tigerfish president, Adam Goldberg, remarked in an email. “We’ve also verified that all of our other S3 buckets are blocked to public access.”.

    “We’re continuing to review and strengthen our storage security more broadly,” added Goldberg.

    The company said that Sen’s email disclosing the data leak was caught in its spam filter.

    According to recent reports, it’s unclear if the firm has notified its customers. Tigerfish did not respond to a follow-up email.

    It has been revealed that discoveries of exposed datasets have consumed a large part of Sen’s early cybersecurity career so far. He scours the web daily using automated scanners and specialist search engines to identify databases, cloud storage, or other sensitive information that likely shouldn’t be left unprotected online.

    Industry observers note that the modern web runs on absolute trust, he mentioned, and operates under the notion that the world’s data is kept secure. But he described how his findings reveal the reality of how “fragile” the internet is behind the scenes.

    Despite the recent focus on how AI is accelerating people’s ability to discover vulnerabilities, Sen remarked that many of the data leaks and exposures that he finds come down to basic human errors.

    “An engineer spinning up a test cloud database on a Friday, disabling authentication to test an API, and forgetting to shut the door before heading into the weekend,” was just one example, he recounted.

    Sen’s findings over the years highlight the ongoing problems caused by such security mistakes, just as the new wave of vibe-coding and AI-generated development is creating new security problems due to insecure and unchecked code deployed to the web.

    Similar to Amazon’s recent efforts to make it difficult to make S3 buckets public without going through clear multistep warnings, newer vibe-coding platforms like Lovable and Supabase have also made changes to their platforms to prevent user mistakes.

    Sources indicate that “Everyone often fears shadowy hackers,” Sen said. But he argues that the real crisis is leaving sensitive systems and databases “wide open to the public internet without a password.”.

    Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

    Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.

    The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.

    Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.

    Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

    It has been revealed that the S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.

    The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.

    Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.

    Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.

    The artificial intelligence (AI) tech giant's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

    Analysts remarked volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the organization was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

    Industry observers note that some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

    Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, noted Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

    While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

    "As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he stated.

    "Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability.".

    Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.

    Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.

    Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it unveiled a bond sale to finance what the organization said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.

    But tech stocks more broadly also fell.

    Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.

    Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - also took a hit.

    Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.

    Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

    South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

    Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

    Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68B

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company.
    • Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
    • Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit.

    Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

    Flash forward to now, with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the fresh cash will be used to repurchase shares.

    Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

    Sources indicate that still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the organization has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable, and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup, and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

    “We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

    Chips can survive the space environment — can their financing?

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
    • The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.
    • In a recent development, those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips?

    The data center ecosystem presently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue.

    In a recent development, those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research, some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024.

    But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the organization’s orbital data center looks. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision.

    That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers.

    However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue.

    In a recent development, musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space.

    Sources indicate that even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts.

    According to recent reports, that might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.

    #47284. Samsung vs. LG OLED TVs: What's the difference between them?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (724 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Samsung vs. LG OLED TVs: What's the difference between them?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (724 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It's not simple to say that one is better than the other.
    • LG and Samsung continue to dominate the OLED TV market.
    • According to recent reports, and you won't find more impressive spec sheets than Samsung OLEDs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It's not simple to say that one is better than the other.

    LG and Samsung continue to dominate the OLED TV market. LG entered the field in 2010 with its humble 15-inch 15EL9500 during the technology's infancy, laying the groundwork for its first 55-inch television in 2012. Throughout the years, LG has slowly built a major foothold in the space with its series of OLED displays. Their crisp colors gives it a unique pop you seldom find in other OLED televisions, even those with more impressive spec sheets.

    According to recent reports, and you won't find more impressive spec sheets than Samsung OLEDs. Since its return to the OLED TV market in 2022, the tech giant has invested heavily in display-panel innovations to carve out its own niche. Samsung's QD-OLEDs are arguably the sharpest-looking OLEDs you'll find in consumer-grade hardware, outperforming LG's panels in color saturation. Based on that, you might think Samsung would be the clear winner for OLED TVs, yet LG's latest OLED innovations make the decision less black-and-white.

    Recent findings suggest that samsung has continued to struggle to provide accurate information about its televisions, obfuscating which panel technologies it uses. LG has faced similar criticism for its major quality concerns with the launch of the G6. Finding the perfect television goes far beyond finding a good panel type. The brand, the television's software and your viewing area should play a key role in your decision.

    It has been revealed that OLED televisions come in three display panel types: WOLED, QD-OLED, and RGB Tandem OLED. WOLED is the most common display type that LG pioneered and continues to innovate on. These TVs use a white light source that passes through four filters to create color: red, green, blue, and white. The white subpixel layer helps brighten the image after it passes through the filters, but it comes at the cost of text clarity. This is the main technology you'll find in LG televisions and is ideal for high ambient-light environments.

    Industry observers note that samsung shook up the OLED space in 2022 with QD-OLED. This technology uses a blue light source that passes through red and green quantum dots. Since the dots convert color rather than filtering it out, these panels tend to have a much wider color gamut and are significantly more energy efficient, which theoretically means they last longer. They're the gold standard for HDR displays, but quantum dot technology makes them ill-suited for bright living spaces; strong light hitting the panel can cause magenta glare.

    Industry observers note that RGB Tandem OLEDs use multiple emissive layers and a striped subpixel layout to boost brightness, reaching upwards of 1,000 nits per pixel on some television models. That stated, the lack of quantum dot technology means RGB Tandems tend to have poorer color accuracy than Samsung's QD-OLEDs. RGB Tandem panels are worth a premium due to the high manufacturing cost.

    On paper, Samsung's QD-OLED seems like the best option for most consumers. You can mitigate nearly all of the panel's weaknesses by minimizing light sources in your viewing space, and its color gamut is best-in-class for consumer televisions. However, the biggest deciding factor for OLED television has nothing to do with the television itself: it's the room you'll use it in. The best QD-OLED television will struggle in a room with high ambient light. And while LG does have some form of anti-glare on its OLED displays, it isn't enough to eliminate reflections entirely.

    Recent findings suggest that software is also a major deciding factor. Samsung's amazing color saturation sadly can't be paired with Dolby Vision, as all Samsung OLED television models lack support for it — HDR10 is their substitute. Additionally, LG and Samsung televisions run different operating systems. LG's WebOS is supported for upwards of five years, while Samsung's latest Tizen OS will receive up to seven years of updates.

    Brand trust shouldn't be disregarded here. Samsung is notorious for poor quality control across its products, including obscuring panel information in certain models. LG has had a more consistent track record, yet it has faced widespread criticism over privacy concerns. The company's terms of service allowed LG to record user conversations and sell them to advertisers. Consumer backlash led the company to release a statement soon after, though many haven't forgiven LG for the controversy.

    Breaking: SpaceX's Starshield troubles in Ukraine could threaten its broader military business

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.
    • According to recent reports, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S.
    • According to recent reports, CNN first reported the letter’s existence.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The representative in the US House expected to chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, Jim Himes (D-Conn.), has threatened to withhold support for funding government-owned systems from SpaceX amid the ongoing inquiry into the use of Starshield in Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “SpaceX’s potentially unilateral modification of a U.S. Government contract, combined with its lack of responsiveness to congressional oversight, calls into question every contract the U.S. Government has with SpaceX,” Himes wrote in a letter to SpaceX founder Elon Musk on Friday.

    According to recent reports, CNN first reported the letter’s existence. The network also reported that Himes sent a classified communication to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton with a similar message that it would be difficult for Congress to authorize funding for systems with SpaceX as the primary vendor.

    SpaceX has developed the consumer Starlink service over the last decade, which provides high-speed Internet from low-Earth orbit to user terminals on Earth. For government customers, SpaceX has also developed Starshield, a suite of satellite services that includes a militarized version of Starlink communications. The US government has purchased Starshield services and extended access to Ukraine, although the terms governing that access are largely classified.

    During the last several weeks, a controversy has erupted over interruptions to Starshield service in parts of Ukraine, cutting off connectivity to drones used to defend against Russian attacks.

    On October 19, for example, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned of Starshield on social media, “Unfortunately, we have established that the equipment stops functioning at speeds of 130–161 kilometers per hour in various sectors of the front. This is slowing down our frontline logistics and limiting the use of various types of drones, particularly mid-strike drones and interceptors of jet-powered ‘shaheds.’” Additional disruptions were reported a week ago.

    The central question is who decided to curtail the performance of Starshield assets in Ukraine. Accounts have variously implicated Musk, SpaceX, the Pentagon, and the White House. Musk has stated that US officials control Starshield access, while defending SpaceX’s right to restrict the use of commercial Starlink service in war.

    Recent findings suggest that “My ask to you is straightforward,” Himes wrote to Musk. “Explain the changes that were made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether those changes were made unilaterally by SpaceX or were directed by a U.S. Government official.”.

    The communications from Himes suggest that Congressional Democrats, who will control the House and Senate in January following decisive victories in the Midterm elections, are prepared to not just investigate the disruption of these SpaceX services in Ukraine, but to take action that could threaten SpaceX’s broader national security business.

    “It is difficult for me to continue supporting the authorization of funding for these SpaceX-developed, government-owned systems, until I receive satisfactory answers to my questions about the Starshield service in Ukraine,” Himes wrote in his letter to Musk.

    Industry observers note that various options are open to Congressional Democrats, as well as some Republicans who have raised similar concerns, including demanding classified briefings and documents and restricting funding through appropriations to the US Department of Defense and other federal departments. Notably, the US Space Force awarded SpaceX a $2.29 billion contract earlier this year to develop the Space Data Network Backbone intended to support the Golden Dome missile defense initiative. That program, along with SpaceX’s work building intelligence satellites for the National Reconnaissance Office, could become a focus of congressional scrutiny.

    According to recent reports, it seems unlikely that the US government would sever ties with SpaceX for space-based data services or releases, as the company is at the moment providing capabilities that no other US company can match. But Democrats are clearly serious about putting restrictions on Musk’s ability to influence geopolitical conflicts that have traditionally been the purview of governments rather than corporations.

    The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio.

    Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.

    The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.

    Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.

    Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.

    Sources indicate that lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.

    All were told they could never serve in the police again.

    Industry observers note that the case became a cause cÃ©lÃ¨bre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.

    Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.

    In a recent development, this was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.

    Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.

    The case was heard by a panel of five judges.

    It has been revealed that the incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.

    They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.

    After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.

    The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.

    During the trial Zecler stated had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.

    In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux noted he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

    #47278. ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2534 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2534 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez states in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.
    • The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food.
    • A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, stated in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez states in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike.

    The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”.

    A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, stated in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

    The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

    Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

    Industry observers note that cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX rolls out rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

    On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

    The next day he indicates six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

    On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS states the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

    On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative indicates neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

    The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

    The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

    Recent findings suggest that the two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

    Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

    Cora Pérez mentioned detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

    “ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

    In a recent development, detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

    “They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez stated in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

    The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

    “I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

    It has been revealed that the Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

    In a statement, DHS stated that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

    Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

    In a recent development, “ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”.

    The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent firm Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

    Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee introduces a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS mentioned that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

    Industry observers note that after a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

    The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant remarked the court had no comment for this article.

    ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

    Recent findings suggest that amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

    Recent findings suggest that “Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan stated. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”.

    Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

    “It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”.

    There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he indicates he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

    It has been revealed that cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

    “He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he remarked.

    The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

    According to recent reports, cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he noted.

    In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative noted. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

    In a recent development, days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then over a year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

    According to recent reports, “All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”.

    In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

    “I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

    “Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

    Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

    “He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

    According to recent reports, cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

    Sources indicate that on 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

    In a recent development, “It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” stated Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”.

    Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he remarked in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

    “[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”.

    Sources indicate that after asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE indicates and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he noted.

    The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

    Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he noted.

    “And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

    As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”.

    #47277. Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (857 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (857 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • "The threat is immense," mentioned Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently.
    • Sources indicate that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added.
    • A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, said Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    "The threat is immense," mentioned Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently. "An estimated cumulative number of 39 million deaths directly attributable to AMR [antimicrobial resistance] would occur in the next 25 years.".

    Sources indicate that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added. "When we see the trend, the investments, the action, we don't think we are on the right track.".

    A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, said Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen. "If antibiotics were no longer effective, modern medicine as we know it today would no longer be possible at all.".

    Imirzalioglu is not only an expert on antibiotic resistance but also on "One Health," a concept adopted in 2004 by experts in human medicine, veterinary medicine and nature conservation. It recognizes that the health of humans, animals and the environment is closely interconnected.

    After all, antibiotics and antimicrobial-resistant germs are not just a problem in hospitals. They can also be found in animal shelters, in animal products, in waste water, in fertilizers and in plants. "One Health tries to keep an eye on all of this," Imirzalioglu mentioned.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    For hospitals and doctors' offices this means that antibiotics must be used as selectively and purposefully as possible. To this end, research is focused primarily on developing better and faster diagnostic methods.

    Industry observers note that in Germany, antibiotics were frequently prescribed against respiratory or urinary tract infections, Imirzalioglu said. But antibiotics are only effective against bacteria. If a virus causes the infection, they are ineffective.

    Nonetheless, every antibiotics dose has consequences: it damages our gut microbiome. This consists of billions of micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, which are essential for digestion, metabolism and the immune system. "If we damage the [bacteria], resistant pathogens can spread and take their place," Imirzalioglu noted.

    Another problem was that such a spreading of resistant pathogens in the gut often went unnoticed and without causing symptoms, he added.

    So people became "carriers of resistant pathogens, which they, in turn, release back into their environment.".

    Industry observers note that in this way, resistant pathogens make their way out of hospitals via toilets and sinks into wastewater and, from there, into the Baltic Sea, where they are ingested by wild birds. This pathway was traced in a study by Katharina Schaufler, a veterinarian and microbiologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health (HIOH).

    Antibiotics have not only been used in humans on a large scale over a long time, excessive use in veterinary medicine has also led to resistance to nearly all available antibiotics, Schaufler noted.

    According to recent reports, in 2006, an EU-wide ban on the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feedcame into effect. Since then, antibiotics may only be applied as part of veterinary treatment.

    The problem is that due to factory farming the use of antibiotics for medical purposes is a permanent necessity. The mere fact that animals live together in confined spaces causes infections to spread rapidly.

    Lack of space as well as boredom lead the animals to injure each other and this happens in an environment where, in Schaufler's words, "there's already a high level of bacterial pressure.".

    Through fertilizers, antibiotic-resistant pathogens enter the environment. "It has been proven that, for example, resistant bacteria can still be found on lettuce heads," the veterinarian remarked. Resistant bacteria were also found time and again on meat.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    National solutions are also falling short. In many countries, antibiotics are still a standard additive in animal feed, Schaufler mentioned. And in such countries, antibiotics could be obtained in drugstores without prescriptions, Imirzalioglu added. Both say that all of this makes the global fight against antibiotic resistance more difficult.

    Political will is of the essence when it comes to combating antibiotic resistance. Imirzalioglu works at Guardian, a project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space.

    The aim of the project is to prevent outbreaks of diseases caused by resistant bacteria by monitoring and analyzing wastewater in the German state of Hesse.

    Recent findings suggest that at EU level, Imirzalioglu is also an advisor at the Antimicrobial Resistance One Health Network. He sums up his experience with policymakers: "The experts and working groups have great ideas, and then these are often scaled back or stifled during the initial stages.".

    Perhaps the lack of political will so far is one of the reasons why the WHO's Nyemazi is issuing an appeal to every individual: Preventing antibiotic resistance means preventing infections, through hygiene, regular vaccinations and doctor's appointments as well as taking medications in accordance with prescriptions.

    This article was originally published in German.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1028 w)

    Super-hot rock geothermal could end data center energy woes

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks.
    • Industry observers note that the broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public.
    • According to recent reports, geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Geothermal startups are in a race to see who can tap the deepest, hottest rocks. The winners could power the next phase of the grid, data centers and all.

    Industry observers note that the broader markets got their first taste of enhanced geothermal earlier this year when Fervo Energy went public. But this week was all about super-hot rock geothermal.

    According to recent reports, geothermal has become a darling among investors, tech companies, and even the Trump administration. The basic technology has been around for decades, but advances in drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry has supercharged it. The U.S. has plenty of potential, too, with up to 57 terawatts of generating capacity, more than enough to power the next wave of AI data centers.

    An emerging class of geothermal energy, known as super-hot rock, could help the industry unlock much of that potential.

    Recent findings suggest that the secret to super-hot rock geothermal is what happens to water at extreme depths. As it gets closer to the superheated core of the Earth, both temperature and pressure rise significantly. When they get high enough, ordinary water turns into a supercritical fluid — a sort of gaseous-liquid state that can carry tremendous amounts of energy. A single super-hot rock well could generate 15 megawatts of electricity or more.

    Industry observers note that super-hot rock geothermal is inching closer to commercial reality. Quaise Energy said on Tuesday that it had landed Google as a customer. The hyperscaler said it would pay more than $500 million to secure 50 megawatts of power from a Quaise project in central Oregon, which will tap into searing heat three miles deep.

    Google is paying a premium for the amount of power Quaise will deliver, but that’s in line with the company’s strategy of getting in early with potential suppliers. For instance, it was an investor in and an early customer of Fervo.

    In a recent development, meanwhile, on Monday, Khosla-backed Mazama Energy declared it had figured out how to keep its drill heads cool as they tap into super-hot rocks. And last week, XGS Energy was given a grant by the Department of Energy to develop and refine materials, well designs, and models to improve reliability at depths where super-hot rock exists.

    XGS is dipping its toes in the super-hot waters, while Mazama and Quaise have made it their core focus, though they’re taking very different approaches.

    Quaise’s technology sounds like science fiction: Starting at about 2.5 miles deep, the company will swap out its conventional drill bit for one powered by a gyrotron, bombarding rock with millimeter-wave radiation and turning it into ash. The hope is that the technology can make drilling under super-hot conditions cost-effective, something that’s challenging with traditional metal drill bits, which wear out faster at those temperatures.

    Mazama, on the other hand, thinks that traditional drill bits will work just fine if they can be kept cool.

    The startup’s newly unveiled technology, Carbon Chill, uses carbon dioxide in place of water-based drilling “mud” to keep the bit cool. At those depths and temperatures, the carbon dioxide turns supercritical, allowing it to hold significant amounts of energy. Just above the drill bit, the CO2 flows through a valve that looks similar to a rocket nozzle. As the gas flows through the valve and expands on the other end, the expansion rapidly cools it, allowing it to absorb significant amounts of heat. The CO2 also removes drill cuttings on its trip to the surface, where it’s filtered and reused.

    In both cases, Quaise and Mazama are betting that their technology could leapfrog today’s state-of-the-art commercial geothermal power plants. By going deeper and hotter, they’re hoping to get substantially more power out of each well. Given that drilling accounts for about a quarter to a third of a geothermal power plant’s total costs, drilling fewer wells could make a project more competitive.

    According to recent reports, investors have been betting that the technologies will soon prove themselves. Quaise has raised more than $270 million from investors, including Prelude Ventures, Collaborative Fund, and Engine Ventures, with Vinod Khosla stepping in as an angel investor, according to PitchBook. Mazama has raised $171 million from investors, including Khosla Ventures, Doerr Capital, and Bill Gates.

    Industry observers note that as with any new technology, there’s some risk that the new techniques won’t pay off. But early results suggest they will — Mazama drilled its second well 80% faster than its first, and its CO2-cooling tech cut drilling time another 20%, co-founder and CEO Sriram Vasantharajan told TechCrunch.

    That, plus Google’s vote of confidence in Quaise, suggests the race to super-hot rock geothermal is, well, heating up.

    #47275. Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (818 w)
    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    Attention Pixel 9 and 10 owners: is it actually worth upgrading to the Pixel 11?

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (818 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that pixel 10 owners can skip this one.
    • Google's new Pixel 11 went on sale in August 2026, but new doesn't always mean better.
    • In a recent development, if the question is whether it's worth upgrading from the 10 to the 11, the answer is no.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that pixel 10 owners can skip this one. Pixel 9 owners have a real decision to make.

    Google's new Pixel 11 went on sale in August 2026, but new doesn't always mean better. It uses the same 6.3-inch display and 5x telephoto camera as the previous year's model; has the same 12GB of RAM; and its battery is just 15mAh bigger. You'll enjoy double the storage space, but it also costs $899, which is $100 more than the launch price of the Pixel 10.

    In a recent development, if the question is whether it's worth upgrading from the 10 to the 11, the answer is no. Keep the phone you've got. If you're a Pixel 9 owner, the advantages are more pronounced. Jumping two generations gets you a telephoto lens, better battery life and an additional two years of software updates, making the upgrade a worthy consideration.

    With the Pixel 11, you get a Tensor G6 chip, which replaces last year's Tensor G5. Google claims the G6 gives users 25 percent improvements in web browsing speed, alongside 15 percent improvements in app debuts. The 48MP main camera gets a larger sensor that's reportedly 56 percent more sensitive to light, and Super Zoom reaches 30x instead of 20x. Wireless charging has increased from 15W to 25W, and the phone now comes with 256GB rather than 128GB.

    In a recent development, while 30x zoom sounds impressive, our hands-on testing found that these zoom shots looked fine on the phone's screen but lost a lot of detail once we opened them on a laptop. The phone itself was quick and fluid, though admittedly nothing we threw at it pushed it very hard.

    Sources indicate that on its comparison page with the Pixel 10, Google lists two camera features as exclusive to the Pixel 11: Magic Capture and Camera Looks. Magic Capture records a short clip and pulls out the best frames as stills, while Camera Looks lets you set and tweak a default filter. However, Android Central's Harish Jonnalagadda argues that most of this year's software additions will reach older Pixels through Google's regular updates anyway. Once you take those away (or, rather, add them to the Pixel 10), you may be essentially paying for a faster chip, double the base memory and quicker wireless charging. That's hard to justify at $899, especially if you bought the Pixel 10 in 2025.

    In a recent development, the Pixel 9 has two rear cameras, a 50MP main and a 48MP ultrawide, and tops out at 8x Super Res Zoom. To that, the Pixel 11 adds a 10.8MP telephoto camera with a 5x optical zoom and optical image stabilization. That's more optical reach than the $799 iPhone 17, which has no telephoto at all, or the $899 Galaxy S26, whose 10MP telephoto stops at 3x. When we reviewed the Pixel 11, that telephoto was its main advantage over phones at the same price. It's not a Pro camera, though. The Pixel 11 Pro's telephoto uses a 48MP, 1/1.95-inch sensor, while the base model makes do with a 1/3.2-inch sensor.

    Industry observers note that in terms of its battery, the Pixel 9 has a 4,700mAh that Google rates for more than 24 hours, while the Pixel 11's 4,985mAh cell is rated for more than 30 hours. In our testing, the Pixel 11 lasted from 8AM on a Saturday to 7PM on Sunday on a single charge. You'll also get Pixelsnap magnets built in with the 11, so magnetic Qi2 chargers and mounts attach without a case, which can't be done with the Pixel 9. The 11's screen is also brighter, peaking at 3,000 nits against the Pixel 9's 2,700.

    Google promises seven years of OS and security updates from the date each Pixel first went on sale in the United States. That puts the end of software updates for the Pixel 9 at August 2031, the Pixel 10 at August 2032 and the Pixel 11 at August 2033, so none of these models are anywhere near being left behind yet. If you're struggling with your Pixel 9's battery life, something which has admittedly led me to prematurely upgrade my phone in the past, a genuine replacement will set you back about $50 at iFixit. Google can also provide price quotes for its mail-in repair service through an online estimator.

    Sources indicate that in our opinion, Pixel 10 owners should definitely consider hanging on until at least the Pixel 12 because, as we noted earlier, you're not getting that much more for your money. The telephoto lens is the real draw for Pixel 9 owners who could benefit from having better zoom — a feature that no software revision can add. But if your Pixel 9 still gets you through the day and you rarely venture beyond 2x zoom, there's no pressing reason to fork out $899 right now.
